McLaren: McLaren has tweaked the underside of the car, reshaping the floor and adding a new rear‑suspension fairing to smooth the airflow and boost down‑force where it counts most. They’ve also fitted a fresh rear wing that grabs extra grip in the corners. Together, these changes should give the team a tighter, more stable platform – the kind of edge that can translate into better corner speeds and stronger tyre life for the upcoming weekend.
Mercedes F1 Team: Mercedes has tweaked the R01’s aerodynamics for this weekend – the side pods now funnel air more aggressively and the nose inlet is larger, while both front and rear wings carry a steeper angle of attack and the front wing has lost its little “fins.” The result is a noticeable boost in downforce, giving the car extra grip in corners and a more stable feel on the straights. In short, the changes should help the team attack the track harder and keep the car planted when the pressure ramps up.
Racing Bulls / RB: Racing Bulls has re‑shaped almost every aero surface to meet the brand‑new 2026 rulebook – the front wing, nose and rear wing now follow the revised layout, and the floor, edge and end‑plates have been re‑profiled. On top of that, the front wing is slimmer but longer and tied into the SM system, the rear wing now has a three‑element active section, and the floor and diffuser have been trimmed and simplified, while the engine‑cover top‑deck and rear‑corner winglets have been reshaped for cleaner airflow and the cooling louvers are tweaked for each circuit. All of these changes give the RB a more balanced downforce package and better cooling, meaning the car should be steadier through the corners and able to extract a little extra grip right out of the box for this weekend’s race.
Aston Martin: Aston Martin has slimmed and reshaped its front wing, adding a tighter three‑element layout and a new dive‑plane endplate, giving the car a sharper “bite” into the corner entry and better airflow to the front tyres. The nose is lifted and split from the wing, while the side‑pod inlets are higher and more forward, feeding cleaner air to the engine and brakes, and the rear has a deeper undercut that carries that airflow straight through to a three‑element rear wing for extra down‑force. In short, the aero package now sticks the car to the tarmac more efficiently, letting the drivers brake later and carry more speed through the bends this weekend.
Haas F1 Team: Haas has reshaped its rear‑end aerodynamics to match the 2026 rulebook: the diffuser now has a tighter, re‑profiled shape, the upper rear wing has been expanded to a three‑element layout (still within a slimmer legal envelope), and the lower “beam” wing has been stripped back to a single, simple piece. These tweaks give the car a cleaner airflow and a more stable rear‑downforce balance, which should translate into better corner grip and more consistent lap times right out of the gate this weekend.
Alpine F1 Team: Alpine rolls out a brand‑new front wing, rear wing and engine‑cover package built to the fresh 2026 rulebook, reshaping the car’s aerodynamics for better grip and stability. The updated wings should give the car more bite in corners while the new bodywork smooths the airflow to the rear, translating into quicker lap times and a stronger fight for points this weekend. In short, the changes aim to make the car feel more planted and responsive when it counts the most.
Audi F1 Team: Audi’s new front‑wing now has two independent actuators, letting each side of the flap move separately for smoother airflow into the car. The side‑pod inlet and body have been reshaped to guide air better toward the floor and rear, creating a “down‑wash” that pushes the car harder into the track. Together these tweaks give the car more consistent grip and stability, which could translate into faster lap times and better tyre wear this weekend.
Cadillac: Cadillac has given the front wing a new flap shape and refined the inner part of its end‑plates, while also re‑working the rear wing’s flap angles. These tweaks tighten the car’s down‑force balance, letting the car stick to the asphalt more consistently through high‑speed corners and under heavy braking. In short, the changes should translate into better grip and stability, giving Cadillac a stronger shot at attacking the podium this weekend.
